issues.title: What happens when publisher sends PUBLISH_DONE?
issues.author: zafergurel
issues.body:
It is not clear about what happens when the original publisher sends a PUBLISH_DONE message for a track in a switching set.
Presumably, the relay should take it out from the switching set and decide which track to send to the subscriber.

comments.author: wilaw
comments.body:
yes. The relay should remove it from the switching set. 

We should add a note to [Relay workflow](https://wilaw.github.io/dts4moq/draft-wilaw-moq-dts4moq.html#name-relay-workflow) to state this.

issues.title: DTS-ACTIVATION in PUBLISH message
issues.author: zafergurel
issues.body: The text says "DTS is enabled and disabled by the subscriber" but the rules are defined by either the subscriber or the original publisher. However, there is nothing in the text that explains how a publisher can set the rules. If it can, the most appropriate message would be PUBLISH IMHO. Also, this makes the use of the word "client" reasonable.

comments.author: wilaw
comments.body: As of today the draft only specifies how the end subscriber defines the sets. There is nothing in the current draft which defines how the original publisher does this. This is not complex and is a planned addition, I just haven't had time to add it yet.

issues.title: remove a track from a switching set
issues.author: gwendalsimon
issues.body:
When reading the text, I struggled to understand the sentence "_The value zero is reserved to indicate no switching set._" in the definition of the switching set. It becomes clearer when reading the paragraph "_To remove one track from a switching set, while leaving the other tracks active, the client issues a REQUEST_UPDATE message with the request ID referencing the subscription it wishes to remove and a SWITCHING-SET-ASSIGNMENT parameter with a Switching set ID of zero._" If we maintain this process, then the first sentence may be rewritten.

That being said, one track can belong to multiple switching sets, can't it? If the Relay receives a switching set 0, should it remove the track from all switching sets? It may be cleaner to have another parameter SWITCHING-SET-STOP-ASSIGNMENT with only the switching set ID.

comments.author: wilaw
comments.body:
No, a track can only belong to one switching set. What is the use-case that requires a track to belong to more than one switching set simultaneously? 

> hen the first sentence may be rewritten.

Suggested rewrite: The value zero is reserved to remove the track from the switching set to which it has been previously added.

comments.author: gwendalsimon
comments.body: All use-cases I had in mind for a track belonging to multiple switching sets can be addressed in a different way, so I close this issue.

issues.title: Limitations of timer-based definition of synchronized tracks
issues.author: gwendalsimon
issues.body:
(As for the SWITCH message), we need a definition of "common group boundaries" for a pair of tracks. I think there is a consensus on a definition such as "_groups with the same ID arriving approximately at the same time_". Yet, timer-based approach has some limitations:
- The Subscriber must set a timeout although it does not know the size of the group, nor the objects. Ex: If the first object of a group takes in average 1 sec to be transmitted, then 200 ms may be acceptable, but it would not be for a small group taking say 50ms to be delivered.
- The Subscriber does not know the Relay upstream connection. In case of significant jitter (for example due to long RTT and non-negligible packet losses), the timer should be increased.
- If the upstream connection is congested, then the track with the minimum bitrate arrives first, maybe by a far margin. In that case, all other high-quality tracks will be unselected because they arrive too late at the Relay.

It could be possible to ignore the "approximately at the same time" to define common group boundaries. We trust the fact that the Subscriber indicated that these tracks are in sync. So if the Relay has the same group IDs for two tracks in its cache or in the upstream wire, it considers they are common group boundaries (and if not, then it is a matter for the Subscriber).

comments.author: wilaw
comments.body:
> The Subscriber must set a timeout although it does not know the size of the group, nor the objects. 

 But it has read the catalog (or some equivalent) so it knows a lot about the bitrate of the tracks and the group spacing and can apply appropriate timeouts. We allow the subscriber to set different duration timeouts for each track to accommodate different expected transfer times. 

> It could be possible to ignore the "approximately at the same time" to define common group boundaries. 

Can you explain how you would do this? If we discard the feature that the switching mechanism will select a second-preference track if the first-preference track does not arrive in time, then we can dispense with timeouts all-together, as the relay will simply make a track selection and stick with it, no matter how long the groups take to arrive. But we have to give up on that feature first.

comments.author: gwendalsimon
comments.body:
> > It could be possible to ignore the "approximately at the same time" to define common group boundaries.
> 
> Can you explain how you would do this? If we discard the feature that the switching mechanism will select a second-preference track if the first-preference track does not arrive in time, then we can dispense with timeouts all-together, as the relay will simply make a track selection and stick with it, no matter how long the groups take to arrive. But we have to give up on that feature first.

The algorithm I had in mind is as follows. A Relay is playing track A (preferred track). It arrives at the end of group N. Then it should take a decision among all tracks for which it received the N+1 group (or if gaps, the N+x  group where x is the smallest). These are the "availableTrackSet". The Relay chooses the preferred track among the availableTrackSet. This set may be similar to the SwitchingSet, or it can be a subset of SwitchingSet due to timing constraints. If A is in the AvailableTrackSet, it can stay on A. It not, then it should choose its preferred track among the AvailableTrackSet.

I think it can avoid one pitfall of the timeout based. Let's say that, because the timer is too strict, some tracks have been "disqualified" for group N+1 (they arrived too late). However, when the Relay arrives at the end of group N, its internal buffer contains the group N+1 for some of these disqualified tracks. Should it ignore these tracks just because they arrived slightly late against a timer some time ago, or should it consider them nonetheless? I would be in the second team. And so we could get rid of the timer.

This was one of the debates related to SWITCH. In my opinion, Groups are "join points". I would say these join points are decision points. The Relay should decide to switch or not when it arrives at the end of a group and should start the next group.

comments.author: wilaw
comments.body: @gwendalsimon After feedback at the Boulder interim, we removed the timer/timeout feature from the implementation. I think that avoids the issues you raised in this issue. If you concur, can you close it?

issues.title: Timer-based algo would need more details
issues.author: gwendalsimon
issues.body:
The algorithm is not completely clear at the Relay side.
- Is the bullet 3 for the initialization only? "_When the first Object 0 of new Group N of track T arrives at the relay_". Should the Relay wait for a first objects of Group N of all tracks to arrive? Is there no timer to start?
-  In bullet 4, "_ If the track T is not the preferred track, then the relay caches the Group of track T and starts a selection timer_". It is not clear when the the selection timer starts. Imho, we should start the timer at the reception of the first packet of the first object of group N+1 in any track, i.e. the first packet to arrive for group N+1 among all tracks in the switching set trigger the selection timer. As said in #6, if we wait for the end of the first object's reception, we are prone to jitter due to the different bitrate across tracks and we advantage to the lowest bitrate (which is probably not what we want). If we use the first byte of the first object, we are less sensitive to timer setting issues.
- In case of gaps, group N+1 should be the next group
- If we finish the transmission of Group N before starting sending the group N+1 (a.k.a. the next group), then we should restrict the approach to ascending order
- The end of the timer may cause problem if the tracks have only *some* group boundaries. It is said that "_If Group N of the preferred track has not arrived by the time the selection timer reaches the selection time limit, then the relay selects a new preferred track [...]_". Let's say that the preferred track A has groups 30, 35, 40 ... and track B has groups 30, 31, 32, 33, 34, 35, 36, ... At the end of Track B's group 30 (or beginning of group 31), the timer would be triggered, which would cause the Track A to be disqualified. Does the Relay stop the delivery of Track A or should it continue the Group 30? If so, what happens at the time of group 35 (track A has been disqualified for 31, 32, 33, 34)?

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Would it make more sense to use the timer like:

Once a track has been selected, it stays selected until the downstream bandwidth no longer permits it OR we haven't received an object from that track from upstream for X ms.  I don't want to restart my timer every group.

MOQT relays without "Rewind" capability have to make a forward/don't forward decision when the object arrives.  It seems like this proposal effectively depends on being able to play back the beginning of an already received group if the preferred track doesn't arrive in time.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
Claude read the algorithm and produced this response:

  The algorithm as I understand it:                                                                       
   
  1. A group boundary is triggered when Object 0 of Group N arrives on any track T in the switching set   
  2. Relay picks the preferred track = highest throughput threshold ≤ estimated throughput              
  3. If T is the preferred track — forward it, done
  4. If T is not the preferred track — cache T's group, start a timer
  5. If the preferred track's Group N arrives before the timer exceeds that track's selection time limit —
   forward the preferred track, done
  6. If the timer expires — remove the preferred track from candidates, re-run selection (go back to step
  2 with a reduced candidate list)

  Things I'm not sure I understand:

  - What happens to cached groups? If Track A's group was cached while waiting for Track B (preferred),
  and B arrives in time — is A's cached data just discarded? And if B doesn't arrive and A gets selected
  via fallback, the cached data is then forwarded?

[this is my question about rewind too]

  - Step 6 recursion — after removing the preferred track and re-running selection, what if the new
  preferred track also hasn't arrived? Do you start another timer? Or is the idea that you only re-select
  among tracks whose groups have already arrived (since they were cached)?
  - "selection timer > selection time limit" — this comparison in step 5 seems backwards (should be <?),
  or maybe I'm misreading the verbatim text. It seems to mean "arrives while the timer hasn't yet exceeded
   the limit."
  - Per-group or per-set timer? There's one timer per switching set per group boundary, right? Not per
  track?

comments.author: wilaw
comments.body:
> What happens to cached groups? If Track A's group was cached while waiting for Track B (preferred),
> and B arrives in time — is A's cached data just discarded? 

No, A is in cache so we just leave it there. With forward=0 subscriptions, all objects normally end up in cache. 

> And if B doesn't arrive and A gets selected via fallback, the cached data is then forwarded?

Yes. 

> Per-group or per-set timer? There's one timer per switching set per group boundary, right? Not per
> track?

There is a separate time limit per track. This group felt that large versus small groups might be expected to have different arrival times. We could simplify things by going to a single time limit per switching set. 

Step 6 recursion — after removing the preferred track and re-running selection, what if the new
preferred track also hasn't arrived? Do you start another timer? 

No. The timer starts just once - when the first object of any Group in the switching set arrives. If the new preferred track hasn't arrived by its time limit, then it too is removed from the  candidate list. 

> "selection timer > selection time limit" — this comparison in step 5 seems backwards (should be <?),

Correct. It should be <.

comments.author: wilaw
comments.body: Based upon the feedback at the Boulder interim, we remove the timer mechanism. That simplifies the implementation . The relay now calculates the preferred track and forwards that, whether it is late or not.

issues.title: lag behind live and cache
issues.author: gwendalsimon
issues.body:
During congestion, the Subscriber lags behind live. It is expected to be less an issue in this adaptive mechanism, but it can still happen. In case the Relay has received several new groups for some tracks, and it cached these groups, should it still refer to the timer result to identify which tracks are qualified for selection?

For example, say that the Relay just finished transmission of group 30. It has in its cache
Track A groups 31, 32, 33. For each of these groups, Track A was the first track to trigger the timer.
Track B groups 31 (arrived before timer expiration), 32 (arrived after expiration), and 33 (arrived before expiration). Track B is the preferred track.

Should the Relay switch to track A for group 31 and back to track B at 32?

comments.author: wilaw
comments.body:
> Should the Relay switch to track A for group 31 and back to track B at 32?

Yes, it should. Group 31 for B was late according to the rules the client set, so the relay sent the next preferred track, which is A.

This assumes the bitrate A < bitrate B. If A> B, then the relay should either send nothing for that group, or send B even though it was late. what do you think?

comments.author: gwendalsimon
comments.body:
> > Should the Relay switch to track A for group 31 and back to track B at 32?
> 
> Yes, it should. Group 31 for B was late according to the rules the client set, so the relay sent the next preferred track, which is A.
> 
> This assumes the bitrate A < bitrate B. If A> B, then the relay should either send nothing for that group, or send B even though it was late. what do you think?

As said in https://github.com/wilaw/dts4moq/issues/6#issuecomment-4084855051, I would prefer ignoring what the timer said some time ago. Here, since I have groups for both tracks, I would choose my preferred track for all groups, regardless of whether they met the timer deadline.

comments.author: wilaw
comments.body:
Based on feedback at IETF #125, I removed all timers with PR #16 . The solution now stays pinned to the preferred track irrespective of how late it is. This largely reflects real world behavior in which tracks will mostly arrive closely to each other. we are only looking for the first byte of each object to be received, not the whole object,so arrival time is relatively decoupled from the size of each object. 


> For example, say that the Relay just finished transmission of group 30. It has in its cache
> Track A groups 31, 32, 33. For each of these groups, Track A was the first track to trigger the timer.
> Track B groups 31 (arrived before timer expiration), 32 (arrived after expiration), and 33 (arrived before expiration). Track B is the preferred track.

With the new implementation, DTS would deliver  B 31. 

If you agree with this, can you close this issue?

comments.author: gwendalsimon
comments.body:
Wonderful! Yes, we can close this issue.
Note that dismissing timer is also in the SWITCH proposal.

issues.title: too many subscriptions in a switching set
issues.author: gwendalsimon
issues.body:
I am not a fan of forcing the Relay to subscribe to many tracks while it only forwards one track downstream. In case of large switching sets, it is a significant burden at the Relay. Furthermore, 99% of the time, Subscribers stick to the highest track, so I hope that the developed clients will not subscribe to all tracks in the altGroup, but only to the subset of tracks that are likely to be used, e.g. the top one (likely to be the preferred one), the second top track (in case of a slight drop of connection) and the lowest (one in case of disaster). 

The dynamic management of switching sets is a great vehicle to save resources at the Relay, but it is in the hand of the Subscriber.

Should we add a mechanism such that
- the Relay declares the maximum number of concurrent subscriptions it can handle in a switching set?
- the Relay rejects a subscription for a switching set because it is above its capacity?

comments.author: wilaw
comments.body:
> Should we add a mechanism such that the Relay declares the maximum number of concurrent subscriptions it can handle in a switching set?

Yes. This could be negotiated in setup. Should it be specified in terms of total bitrate or just track count? For example, switching 3x2160p video tracks takes a lot more resources than 10 x 32kbps audio tracks.

comments.author: gwendalsimon
comments.body:
> > Should we add a mechanism such that the Relay declares the maximum number of concurrent subscriptions it can handle in a switching set?
> 
> Yes. This could be negotiated in setup. Should it be specified in terms of total bitrate or just track count? For example, switching 3x2160p video tracks takes a lot more resources than 10 x 32kbps audio tracks.

I would suggest both.
Subscribing to tracks is a burden both in terms of cache storage and in terms of subscription management. So, I would prefer having the option to have two limits: max total kbps, and max number of tracks in the Switching set.

issues.title: First preferred track
issues.author: gwendalsimon
issues.body:
The text says that (in the third bullet) that "_When the first Object 0 of new Group N of track T arrives at the relay, the relay selects the preferred track to forward from the switching set. The preferred track is the track with the highest throughput threshold smaller than or equal to the current throughput estimate._" I think it is for the first choice of preferred track. However, the Relay does not know the current throughput estimate (unless it already has a downstream connection to the same Subscriber).

It could be possible to let the Subscriber indicate the preferred track in the Switching-Set-Assignment with a flag "default-preferred-track" which says that the subscription is about the track that should be chosen first at the activation.
if several tracks are noted as preferred one, then the last one is chosen.
It no track is noted as preferred one, then the Relay chooses any of them.

comments.author: wilaw
comments.body:
> However, the Relay does not know the current throughput estimate (unless it already has a downstream connection to the same Subscriber).

It is my understanding that immediately after the connection is established, and before the client issues any subscribe requests, that the relay has some estimate of the throughput. It may be application limited, but its still an estimate. It is likely a lower estimate since only the opening setup has been conducted, but this means that the ABR would start low and then switch up, which is the safer behavior.

comments.author: gwendalsimon
comments.body:
OK, it is consistent with the principle of server-side ABR. Only the Relay takes the decision and the client is passive. Even for a default preferred one. 
So I close this issue.

issues.title: Activate operates on a set, not a single subscription
issues.author: afrind
issues.body:
This shouldn't be a REQUEST_UPDATE parameter, but a new message?  In draft-17, that means it would need it's own bidi stream too.  You could get rid of "off" in that case - cancelling the bidi stream is implicit off.

Or we could live with the awkwardness of applying to a subscription -- is it an error if the subscription doesn't belong to the activated set?

comments.author: wilaw
comments.body:
> This shouldn't be a REQUEST_UPDATE parameter, but a new message? 

Why a new message? The DTS-ACTIVATION parameter exists for two reasons:
1. It tells the relay when to begin applying the track selection logic. Practically, this will nearly always be after it has done subscribing to the last track in the set, therefore having it as a parameter that can accompany a SUBSCRIBE makes sense. For this use case, we could just add a bit flag to the SWITCHING-SET-ASSIGNMENT parameter, to say "I'm done defining tracks, start switching", rather than a separate parameter. 
2. It tells the relay when to stop applying the track selection logic AND continue subscribing to the streams. One can argue that this is a non use-case and that the client will always want ot have those tracks in ABR mode, in which case the client can just unsubscribe from each track in the set in order to cancel the ABR. I quite like this approach as it simplifies things.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: I don't object to the signal - just noting that this not specific to a subscription.

comments.author: wilaw
comments.body:
Note that the implementation has been updated to remove the DTS-ACTIVATION parameter. There is now a single [parameter](https://wilaw.github.io/dts4moq/draft-wilaw-moq-dts4moq.html#name-switching-set-assignment-pa) which has the activate-switching flag. Your original points still hold however. We felt the "awkwardness" of it being applied to a subscription update but being intended to modify a switching set was less than the complexity of creating a new Message type. Additionally, for the Message proposal , cancelling the bidi stream would delete the switching set, instead of just pausing it as the current Api does. 

```
SWITCHING-SET-ASSIGNMENT {
  Switching set ID (v64),
  Throughput threshold (v64),
  Set throughput fraction (v64),
  Activate switching (1),
  [Set rank (8)]
}
```

>  is it an error if the subscription doesn't belong to the activated set?

yes.

issues.title: Bandwidth estimates are per connection
issues.author: afrind
issues.body:
The algorithm seems to assume that the switching set consumes the entire bandwidth of the connection, but there are likely other tracks.

How does the subscriber communicate the fractional share of bandwidth allocated to a given switching set?  e.g. 5 meeting participants with 3 video tracks each, plus audio tracks.

comments.author: wilaw
comments.body:
> The algorithm seems to assume that the switching set consumes the entire bandwidth of the connection,

This is true. 

> How does the subscriber communicate the fractional share of bandwidth allocated to a given switching set? e.g. 5 meeting participants with 3 video tracks each, plus audio tracks.

We can add a new field to the switching set definition which is the fractional share that should be allocated to this set? In the example above, this would be 5. The relay would take its estimate of the connection throughput, divide that by 5, and use that fraction as the throughput value it applies to each switching decision.

issues.title: Describe how the scheme works when publisher has to unpublish some tracks in a switching set due to constrained uplink
issues.author: gchandok
issues.body: Subscriber may have set up a switching set include all track variants and publisher may be actively sending those. Now if the publisher's uplink throughput drops it may have to stop sending one or more tracks in the set. We should document how would the relay and the subscriber react to this. Ideally the relay would start sending the highest variant the the publisher is publishing but this may need some signaling between subscriber and relay

comments.author: wilaw
comments.body:
If a publisher stops sending a track that is part of a subscriber-defined switching set, then the relay MUST remove that track from the set and perform switching between the remaining tracks in the set. Same is true if the set was constructed via SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE. The terminated track would simply fall out of the Track Filter. 

You make a good point that the relay will remove the  terminated track form the set, and that this is not something that the subscribing client would need to do.

issues.title: Feedback from IETF#125
issues.author: wilaw
issues.body:
1. Remove the Selection time limit attribute from the SWITCHING-SET-ASSIGNMENT parameter. The feeling was that this complicated the implementation. It's utility is to enable the relay to select a lower bitrate track if the preferred track arrives late. The group felt that this would occur infrequently enough and if it did, then the existing delivery timeout feature of MOQT would kick-in and the client could remove the offending track from the switching set.

2. Remove the DTS-ACTIVATION parameter and replace its functionality with a flag in the SWITCHING-SET-ASSIGNMENT parameter.

issues.title: Clarify the applicability of DTS for layered coding
issues.author: zaheduzzaman
issues.body: Based on our discussion at IETF125, it should be made clear that the DTS is not desinged for trackes with layered coding, as the base layer cannot be switched. For that case one way of doing it is to use track priority.

comments.author: wilaw
comments.body:
@zaheduzzaman  - PR #16 added the language 

> For tracks to participate in a dynamic switching set, they:
> 
> * MUST be time aligned at group boundaries.
> * MUST hold equivalent and independent versions of the same content, encoded at different bitrates. DTS is not a solution for switching between Scalable Video Coding (SVC) layers.

issues.title: How do you allocate bandwidth for non-DTS switched tracks?
issues.author: afrind
issues.body: If I read the latest draft correctly, each switching set gets a fraction (weight), but there's an assumption that sum(weights) across all switching sets normalizes to "all available bandwidth".  Or did I misunderstand?

pulls.title: Add use-cases
pulls.author: suhasHere
pulls.body: This PR adds a list of use-cases where DTS for MOQ is very useful and helps drive the requirements as well.

comments.author: wilaw
comments.body:
HI @suhasHere  - i like these use-cases, but the text is very long, longer in fact than the draft itself. This impairs the readability of the draft for those interested in the mechanics of its implementation. Can you move these to an appendix and then reference them in the introduction section? 

Reading through them all, the one feature that we need to add (which I hinted at in the IEFT#125 presentation), is to add a "fractional" or weight attribute for each switching set, to allocate what fraction of the total connectivity should be allocated to each switching set, along with a mechanism to easily update this. I will add this in my post #125 PR.

````suggestion
ensure text remains readable. The relay manages bandwidth allocation between the two content types,
````

````suggestion
subscribes to all tiles within the field of view and as gaze direction changes, subscriber
````

While it is fine for the subscriber to indicate the weigth or fraction of the connection which a particular set should consume, we already have the SUBSCRIBER_PRIORITY parameter in MOQT for SUBSCRIPTIONS. Adding in another layer of priority via DTS will complicate things and should be avoided. The client can express priority using the existing priority mechanisms.
Priority should not be adjusted via DTS.
Would prefer to leave priorities out of DTS.
The relay SHOULD allocate based on relative weights/fractions, but can honor the priority originally assigned to the subscription.

pulls.title: Remove the DTS-ACTIVATION parameter & add fractional support.
pulls.author: wilaw

comments.body: Having two integer (numerator and denominator) would be better. I typically want to use 4/5th of my bandwidth for video
+1. we need to have num/den so that that resulting number is <1

I agree. I think if we allow specification  as any numerator/denominator than we imply a degree of precision which the relay cannot achieve. Allocating bandwidth is very difficult for a relay to do accurately. Specifying a fraction of 48/77 is unlikely to be met, but specifying a more general target of 60% 

Instead, I propose that we allow the fraction to be specified in increments of 10%, from 10% to 100%. This reduces the precision but a) can be expressed as a single number N/10 and b) More closely matches the precision which the relay is likely to be able to obtain. c) gives you enough real world ability to shard bandwidth between sets. 

I have gone ahead and made this change with commit https://github.com/wilaw/dts4moq/pull/16/changes/e593743be51247e877ceff5b25e9ece7398e55b0.

Let me know if this satisfies your requirement.

pulls.title: Add support for single and multiple switching sets in DTS
pulls.author: suhasHere
pulls.body:
This PR allows Subscribers to create multiple switching sets through two methods via Individual SUBSCRIBEs and  SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE with TRACK_FILTER, wherein both methods result a similar relay behavior

It further:

- Updates introduction and abstract to refer to the use-cases
- Clarifies Mapping model from MOQ Tracks to Switching Sets
- Explain unified relay behavior for single and multiple switching sets and shows from the relay perspective the behavior is same
- Adds optional set rank for cases where sets need not be degraded equally. 
- Provides examples explaining the proposal
- Add a section on how SWITCH and DTS interact or can be supported in a single solution

comments.author: suhasHere
comments.body: @wilaw  the new sets of commits should be good to do. Please check with all comments turned off.

reviews.author: wilaw
reviews.body:
I have two main concerns:
1.  The definition and behavior of how Fraction and Rank work together
2. Why the section on comparison to SWITCh is in this draft.

See individual comments on both these subjects, along with others.

comments.body:
```suggestion
switching set and specifies bandwidth allocation and optional ranking.
```
What error is returned if this track is already subscribed to a switching set?

This can also be used to pause switching, even if more subscriptions will not be added. 

```suggestion
* **Activate switching**: 0 to deactivate switching or 1 if the
  relay should activate switching. The change takes place at the next group boundary. 
```

What if you assign Set 1 from track A with a throughput fraction of 4 and then assign Set 1 for Track B with a throughput fraction of 2. Which takes precedence?

I think the last specified should take precedence. If so, that should be stated in the definition.

The interplay between fraction and rank is unclear as defined. Based upon the algorithm defined at line 585, the set with the highest rank is treated as if its fraction were 100% of the available bandwidth. Only for sets with equal rank, do the fractions then count. This fact should be made clear in the definitions of both set fraction and set rank. Currently the details are buried in pseudo-code.

Let's imagine we have two switching sets, the first #1 assigned a 60% fraction and the second #2 a 40% fraction. #1 is given a rank of 10 and #2 is given a rank of 1 (highest). 

Lets say the estimated throughput is 10Mbps. So Set #2 is switched as if it has 100% of the available bandwidth allocated to it. Once the track is selected, that bandwidth is subtracted from the available bandwidth and then set #1 is switched.

What happens if Set#2 (highest rank) consumes all of the available bandwidth? There will be nothing left for lower ranked sets. Do they not get delivered at all? The answer is probably yes, and this should be made clear in the description.

No, the first thing it must do is either a) allocate all of the bandwidth to the highest rank set or b) Divide the available bandwidth based upon the fraction of the sets if there are 2 or more sets with equal highest rank.

Lets imagne we have Set#1 with 80% fraction and a rank of 1, then sets #2 and #3 with 10% fraction each and a rank of 2.

Set#1 will be switched first, and the remaining bandwidth will be allocated to #2 and #3. Does each get switched as if they have 10% of the remaining bandwidth (because that is what is defined  for each) or 50% (because they are equal at 10% so the bandwidth gets shared between them). I think your intended behavior is the latter, i which case this algorithm needs to get adjusted. 

B_set  = B_total x (N*10/Sum(N for all sets with this rank))
Is the relay expected to detect and react to SCONE metadata?
Not immediately. It would occur at the next group boundary, which might be one second away.

Not really. It protects the main camera by allocating all available bandwidth to that set, switching it, then giving the left-over bandwidth to the replay camera. This degradation happens second in the algorithm, not first. The replay camera degrades as a consequence of the main camera receiving higher priority.

SWITCH is not only about adapting due to bitrate. The SWITCH proposal clearly explains that the track switch may be use to discretionary use-inout, such as selecting a particular race-car camera from a grid view. This has nothing to do with with bandwidth adaption and is not address by DTS.
No, they also address switching based on other client-side requirements.

DTS requires an active subscriuption ot all tracks in a set. SWITCH does not. 

There are many cost reasons why a distributor may not want to have all clients pull all tracks to the edge relay.
For SWITCH it is 1/2 RTT. The message processing is effectively instant. IN most cases, this 1/2 RTT is < distance to group boundary, so switching takes place at the same time in both cases.

You should also add a line for "Client flexibility". With SWITCH, the client can adjust its algorithm at any time and have complex ABR algorithms that take into account many factors. The Relay implementation via DTS is very simple in comparison and not easy to update, as it requires coordinating software updates across multiple third party provider.
DTS does not provide equivalent functionality to SWITCH. DTS only works with bandwidth based-switching. SWITCH can work with your head-position for example in a VR application.

I don't think this whole section should be in this draft, which is a definition of DTS. If you want to compare DTS with SWITCH, that can be done in an informational draft somewhere else. 

I suggest removing this entire section from the document.

This section should be removed.

I am frankly quite upset by it, because it does not simply compare DTS and SWITCH; it misrepresents SWITCH and, in doing so, dismisses core requirements of live streaming.

First, this is not specification text. It reads as advocacy for DTS inside a DTS draft. Will is right: if the authors want to compare DTS and SWITCH, that belongs in a separate informational document, not here.

Second, the claim that DTS provides “equivalent functionality” to SWITCH is false, and the comparison is misleading on both control model and resource model. DTS requires active subscriptions to all renditions in a switching set, plus relay-side bandwidth estimation and decision-making for each downstream connection. SWITCH does not. This is not a minor implementation detail; it is a fundamentally different architecture. And DTS is a poor one from a resource-efficiency standpoint: K renditions have to be kept at the relay so that only 1 can be used, and the relay must maintain per-connection estimation and adaptation logic. That is an obvious waste of bandwidth, state, and processing at the edge. Forward=0 does not solve that problem; it only avoids downstream forwarding of the non-selected tracks. Someone has to pay for that waste, and I seriously doubt the streaming industry will accept to pay for such a mechanism.

Third, the section ignores an essential requirement of live streaming: the client may deliberately choose not to switch during a temporary throughput drop because it still has buffer to absorb it. This is exactly why SWITCH includes Joining FETCH semantics and allows the subscriber to account for buffered content and drift from the live edge when switching. DTS, by contrast, is designed to keep the decision at the relay and very close to the live edge. That is a fundamentally different model. Pretending that the two are equivalent shows a real lack of respect for how live streaming actually works in the industry.

In short: this section is misplaced, technically inaccurate, and should be removed.

@gwendalsimon  @wilaw you are both correct. My intention was not to say switch is replaced by DTS, but wanting to see if we can get funcionality of it over DTS. Here is my rough thinking ( which i should have share before adding it to PR)


@wilaw raised a valid point that SWITCH supports non-bandwidth criteria
  (e.g., VR gaze tracking). However, DTS already provides mechanisms for
  subscribers to influence relay decisions based on application-specific
  context—the relay doesn't need to understand those criteria directly.

  The subscriber retains full control over which streams matter and how
  much bandwidth each should receive. The relay only handles the
  bandwidth-constrained selection within those parameters.

  Example: VR head-position tracking with DTS

  // User looks at tile 3 → subscriber promotes it
  REQUEST_UPDATE (tile3) fraction=4   // high priority
  REQUEST_UPDATE (tile1) fraction=1   // demote others

  // User looks at tile 5 → subscriber adjusts
  REQUEST_UPDATE (tile3) fraction=1   // demote
  REQUEST_UPDATE (tile5) fraction=4   // promote new gaze target

  The subscriber's application logic (gaze tracker, active speaker
  detector, etc.) runs locally and translates application-specific
  signals into DTS parameters. The relay then makes optimal bandwidth
  allocation decisions within those constraints.

  Key difference from SWITCH: With SWITCH, the subscriber must also run
  bandwidth estimation and ABR selection. With DTS, the subscriber only
  expresses intent (via fractions/priorities), and the relay handles
  bandwidth-optimal execution. This separation means:
  - Subscriber logic is simpler (no ABR algorithm needed)
  - Relay can react faster to bandwidth changes (no RTT delay)
  - Application-specific criteria are still fully supported
  
  
  Please let me know if this addresses all the requirements for SWITCH. I am happy to learn it doesn't and not proceed in this direction too. please let me know

Thanks, Suhas. I appreciate the clarification.

In live streaming, we do NOT want to react to every bandwidth change. A temporary throughput drop should often be absorbed by the client buffer rather than trigger an immediate downgrade. Faster reaction is not better; it makes the system more nervous and degrade quality unnecessarily.

Furthermore, we WANT the client to run the ABR logic. The client is the entity that knows the relevant playback context: buffer level, playback rate, distance from the live edge, recent delivery history, and rebuffer risk. The relay does not. A relay-side bandwidth estimate plus a few subscriber hints is not equivalent to client-side ABR.

This is also why lag behind live is a feature, not a bug. In live streaming, keeping some controlled distance from the live edge is what allows the client to absorb transient bandwidth reductions without unnecessary switching. That is why Joining Fetch MUST exist in SWITCH.

Finally, the resource model of DTS is poor. DTS keeps K renditions active at the relay so that only 1 is actually used, and it adds one bandwidth estimation and adaptation loop per downstream connection. That is a waste of bandwidth, state, and processing at the edge. Someone has to pay for that design, and I am not convinced the streaming industry will accept such a costly mechanism, with respect to the size of the ladder (K=9 is not unusual) and the bitrates of the tracks.

> // User looks at tile 3 → subscriber promotes it
> REQUEST_UPDATE (tile3) fraction=4 // high priority
> REQUEST_UPDATE (tile1) fraction=1 // demote others
> 
> // User looks at tile 5 → subscriber adjusts
> REQUEST_UPDATE (tile3) fraction=1 // demote
> REQUEST_UPDATE (tile5) fraction=4 // promote new gaze target

This argument doesn't work if the subscriber is switching from an English audio track to a French one. IN the example above, the demoted tiles (or language) have a fraction of 1 and are still delivered. But thats not want we want. We want a clean switch from English to French where one replaces the other. If the argument is that the fraction can be set to 0, then we are just re-inventing forward=0 as well as unsubscribe, both of which we already have. I see SWITCH and DTS serving different purposes and I feel MOQT needs both to offer the most flexibility to applicantion architects.

```suggestion
  the fraction value is ignored unless two or more sets have the same rank value; in which case the available bandwidth is allocated between those sets according to their fractions. If each rank only holds one set, then allocation is determined entirely by rank order.
```
